title: bin/lib/ — six primitives, fourteen implementations, no shared module
from: MEASURED, so this is a defect class and not tidiness. Six primitives, fourteen implementations: write_atomic in perry-conform + perry-decide + perry-migrate; load_schema in perry-decide + perry-conform + perry-task; resolve_state_root in perry-diagnose + viewer/parsers.py; project_lock and mint_id each in perry-decide + perry-task; heading_re in perry-lint + perry-task. EVERY REVIEW ROUND THIS SESSION FOUND AN INSTANCE OF EXACTLY THIS. squash versus .strip().lower() across bin/ and viewer/ (TASK-050, still open, silently loses a user's live risks). The writer's is-this-a-risk-table predicate being a second copy of the reader's. split_stages in two files. norm being squash under another name. Each was fixed one at a time; the structure that generates them was not touched. There is no shared module, so a second implementation is the path of least resistance every time. THE PATH HACK IS THE OTHER HALF. Eight sys.path.insert calls: seven tools reverse-import from viewer/, and three of them re-insert bin/ to import each other. viewer/parsers.py is 2,520 lines — the second-largest file in the repo — and it is the read side of every CLI tool while living in a directory named for the web viewer. tests/ imports it the same way. Whether it moves out of viewer/ or viewer/ stops being the anchor is the decision to make and state. THE GATE: behaviour-neutral. The suite is the proof and no test may need editing — that is what made the viewer/tables.py extraction safe, and it is the property to reproduce. from: viewer/parsers.py normalizes header cells with .strip().lower() at 11 sites; bin/perry-task and bin/perry-lint use squash, which also strips backticks and asterisks. On a header whose Risk cell is bolded, the writer says risk-table and the reader says not — so risk-add writes, perry-state reports 0 risks, perry-lint is clean and risk-migrate says already migrated. Four exits, all closed. Task tables survive only via positional fallbacks. to: SECOND-ROUND FIX 2026-08-18, after the V4 review FAILED this on the CATEGORY. The first pass unified viewer/parsers.py and reported done; the reviewer found THREE surviving second implementations in files that never imported squash — bin/perry-state twice (the Tracks header and the pack glossary header) and bin/perry-diagnose once (md_table, which reads the USER's board and OKR). from: BLOCKING FINDING FIXED 2026-08-18. The V4 re-review scored all five guarantees and found ADR-004 DOES NOT REOPEN — dry run complete and byte-identical to a cold apply, 0 ids and 0 characters lost across 30 files (mutation-tested: patching edit.after to drop a line made all 30 refuse with 0 bytes on disk), restore returns every file byte-identical, one declaration record via perry-conform, and partial migration behaves as designed. The one blocker was guarantee 3's failure path: only a write that LANDED WRONG was handled, so a write that FAILS — read-only file, full disk, permission revoked mid-run — propagated as an unhandled traceback, leaving a stranger's project N-of-M migrated with the restore point on disk and NEVER NAMED, the declaration never run, and empty stdout. A traceback names nothing. FIXED: the write is caught, the run is rolled back, and rollback_message names the restore point path and the exact recover command. THE PART THAT MATTERED MOST: undo() writes too, so the failure that broke the run can break the repair — the path is therefore named FIRST and unconditionally, and whether the automatic rollback succeeded is reported as a separate fact, so the worst case is not the one case that tells the user nothing. Also fixed: apply on a project with nothing writable raised KeyError 'run' in the renderer. 4 mutations red. gimegime-pmo 59 to 15 unchanged. AWAITING a fresh V4 on the fix.
to: V4 ROUND 3: FAIL on guarantee 3, ADR-004 STANDS — fixed 2026-08-18. The reviewer stopped guessing where the third crash was and ENUMERATED ALL FIVE PLACES MIGRATION WRITES TO A PROJECT. Rounds 1 and 2 had guarded two; three were unguarded, including the recovery path itself: do_restore's undo restored BOARD.md and then died unlinking conformance.md, leaving it half restored with the record still claiming conformance for a rolled-back file — the exact thing restore_point's own docstring exists to prevent. C.declare sat outside round 1's try, so a project migrated once and then locked down was FULLY migrated with the restore point on disk and never named. restore_point itself was unguarded. THE AXIS ALL THREE ROUNDS MISSED: a read-only DIRECTORY, not a read-only file — write_atomic renames, and a rename needs write permission on the directory, which is why every existing test, all driving read-only through a file, passed throughout. FIXED all three plus the scratch write in Linter.errors, guarded rather than exempted because an exemption list is where this kind of guard rots. AND THE ENUMERATION IS NOW A STANDING CHECK: tests/test_migrate.py TestEveryWriteSiteIsGuarded walks the AST and fails if any write call sits outside a try — proved by planting a sixth site after the guard was written and watching it go red. That is the fix; the three patches are not. Guarantees 1, 2, 4, 5 all PASS on gimegime-pmo (365 to 380 ids, none lost, 59 to 15, 30 declared, PolyForge refused in one sentence). TASK-079 affects guarantee 4 and not 3 — restore puts the read-only file's bytes back exactly; what the preview never mentions is the mode it is about to override. AWAITING a fresh V4.

from: SECOND-ROUND FIX 2026-08-18, after the V4 review FAILED this on the CATEGORY. The first pass unified viewer/parsers.py and reported done; the reviewer found THREE surviving second implementations in files that never imported squash — bin/perry-state twice (the Tracks header and the pack glossary header) and bin/perry-diagnose once (md_table, which reads the USER's board and OKR). Writing the category-shaped guard then found a FOURTH nobody had named: bin/perry-explain resolved headers with strip_md(c).lower(), a rule that differs from squash on internal whitespace — AND split rows with m.group(1).split('|'), a fifth splitter that does not honour the escape. Neither was reachable by TASK-050's or TASK-067's guards because BOTH were written against a hardcoded file list that did not name that file. THE DIVERGENCE IS REAL, not theoretical: '**Default** rung' lowers to 'default** rung' and matches nothing, so a project that bolded half a header lost the column silently and every track reported no default rung. Fixed at all four sites, header-only — the value normalizers (Status, Outcome, parse_frequency) keep their own rules deliberately, because they normalize what a project WROTE rather than which column it wrote it in, and widening the guard to cover them flags eight correct call sites. tests/test_one_header_rule.py holds the category: no reader builds a lowercased list over a row's cells, every table reader reaches squash, and perry-lint's norm alias is asserted to BE squash so it cannot quietly become a fifth copy. 4/4 mutations red. Suite 1075 to 1081. AWAITING a fresh V4.
to: V4 ROUND 3: FAIL. The decisive test the spec demanded — plant a new reader — came back GREEN, which IS the finding. The reviewer planted two plausible readers at HEAD, each resolving a header with strip-backtick-lower and carrying its own splitter: TASK-050's guard green, the decoration guard green, only TASK-067's guard red and only on the SPLITTER, never on the header rule. Three isolated blind spots, each measured separately: (1) SUBDIRECTORY — the byte-identical file is green at bin/lib/rows.py and red at bin/perry-rows-probe, because READERS uses iterdir plus is_file; this is the exact defect that had JUST been fixed in the sibling guard, unfixed one file over, and bin/lib is the directory TASK-065 exists to create. (2) SPELLING NOT SHAPE — 'for c in cells' red, 'for h in header' green; one variable rename walks past. (3) viewer/ is still a hardcoded one-file list, and the complement test skips any file lacking split_row, which exempts exactly the own-splitter-plus-own-header-rule combination that bit in perry-explain. AND A FIFTH LIVE COPY, found by AST over all 111 lowercasing sites: viewer/parsers.py read_conformance stripped backticks and spaces and LEFT ASTERISKS, so a bolded File header was read as a declaration and perry-conform status reported unreadable row against a correct file while perry-lint said clean. WHY FOUR COPIES SURVIVED THREE ROUNDS: the behavioural guard's fixture bolds WHOLE CELLS, and on whole-cell decoration the two rules AGREE — so exactly one guard can see the rule that shipped, and it is the one a new reader walks past. FIXED 2026-08-18: the fifth copy now uses squash, with plain/bolded/quoted/padded headers asserted identical, mutation red. STILL OPEN: all three guard blind spots.

from: DEFINITION CHANGED 2026-08-18 by ADR-006 (decide lane, user-decided). THIS ROW NO LONGER BUILDS WHAT ITS TITLE SAYS. DESIGN-005 section 6 step 4 now reads: the TASK STORE becomes canonical (perry/tasks.jsonl), BOARD.md becomes a projection, and the event log STAYS A LOG. Previously it read 'the event log becomes canonical', which fused two things section 4 never fused — decision #1 chose a structured store for tasks, decision #2 chose JSONL, and neither said the store and the log are one file. Section 5.2 did, on the stated ground of keeping ADR-002 satisfied, and ADR-002 is 'no cross-project registry' with no clause against a file inside a project and an explicit exemption for .perry/events.jsonl. The only reason given for one file was a citation that does not say what it was cited for. MEASURED BEFORE DECIDING: every full-set read is O(events) — 173 events for 75 tasks, a ratio that only rises — and 57 percent of the log's bytes are next events, cell overwrites with no replay value, in the file that must be traversed to answer section 1.3's own question. THREE LAYERS TO BUILD: perry/tasks.jsonl as truth (one object per task, current state, rewritten in place, under the STATE ROOT not .perry/ — location is the claim); BOARD.md as the rendered open subset; .perry/events.jsonl as history, append-only and disposable AGAIN. Still P1, still V5, still last of the four steps — the sequencing did not move, only what gets built. perry-task/list keeps its shape: where a value is read from is not a contract fact.

to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19, after its round-4 FAIL. The header rule dies for BOARD.md, OKR.md and .perry/config.md when TASK-094 deletes it — those files stop being tables. What REMAINS in this row's scope is design/*.md and .perry/roles/*.md, and under ADR-007 rule 2 Python stops parsing those entirely rather than resolving their headers correctly. So the four rounds of guard-versus-reviewer on this row are not worth a fifth: the category is being removed, not hardened. from: ALL ROUND 3 FINDINGS FIXED 2026-08-18, awaiting a fresh V4. Both decisive tests already passed in round 3 — a planted f-string writer and a planted raw-splitter reader were BOTH caught, and a hand-destroyed row reports ragged-row where it used to report clean. Criterion 1's two gaps are now closed: append_cell collapsed a line break at rc 0 where check_cell two functions above raises, and double-escaped a pipe on its re-render branch so the same value stored two ways depending on whether the row ended in a pipe — both halves now route through check_cell, four tests, two mutations red; and the refusals in perry-task and perry-goals printed the character but never the FIELD, so --next and --title gave identical messages — the offending value is now matched back to the argument that carried it, exact match only, because naming the wrong flag is worse than naming none. THE GUARD'S OWN BLIND SPOT, which the reviewer said it would flag hardest: _tools() used iterdir plus is_file and a non-recursive glob, so NO SUBDIRECTORY WAS VISIBLE and nine planted files stayed green, including bin/lib/rows.py — the directory TASK-065 exists to create. It walks the tree now, and HAND_ROW_RE matches an interpolation anywhere in the row rather than only in the first cell. AND ragged-row reported the SECTION HEADING's line rather than the row's: tables_with_lines is now the real scanner and tables() a view of it, verified with two ragged rows at known different lines because one sample cannot tell a constant offset from a coincidence — my first fix matched rows back by id() across two calls that build different objects and changed nothing, and my second was off by one. OUT OF SCOPE, as the reviewer recorded: the WHY/catalog entry, since the repo's catalog convention covers perry-diagnose ids only and that clause of criterion 5 is ambiguous.
to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19, after its round-4 FAIL. Once the three stores land, no markdown cell holds a value — so a writer cannot destroy a table it no longer writes, and a reader cannot mis-split a row that is not a row. The static guard that four rounds could not make category-shaped stops needing to be category-shaped. WHAT SURVIVES: adoption of a foreign project, which parses by definition, and that is where this row's remaining scope goes. The behavioural backstop (tests/test_escaped_pipe_corpus.py) survives too and is the right shape for it. KEEP OPEN until TASK-094/095 land.

title: perry-goals writer
from: ALL FIVE ROUND 3 FINDINGS FIXED 2026-08-18, awaiting a fresh V4. (1) The central one: render_row and check_cell were TWO guards while the docstring said one — splitlines splits on eleven boundaries and the membership test on two, so six characters were refused on create and accepted on amend. line_break_at() is now the single rule and a test forbids either caller from spelling the test itself; the six are enumerated FROM THE LANGUAGE, not from the bug report, which named two. (2) Refused was raised in viewer/tables.py and defined nowhere in it, reachable through --close/--miss on a Commitments table with no Status column, giving a NameError where a refusal belongs; it now raises this module's own exception. (3) A refusal names the FLAG — index is a column position and means nothing to the person who typed the command, so --next and --title gave identical messages; the offending value is matched back to the argument that carried it, exact match only. (4) Whitespace-only was refused on create and ERASED the cell on amend, because that branch tested is-not-None where the other strips; --discharged-by is deliberately excluded and a test pins that exclusion. (5) append_separator_cell assumed a trailing pipe where append_cell handles its absence, so a widen produced a 7-cell header against a 6-cell separator at rc 0 with lint silent. Every fix mutation-verified. TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WERE FAKE AND MUTATIONS CAUGHT BOTH: one asserted the whitespace guard's source construct existed and stayed green when the condition inside it became if-False, rewritten at CLI level against the file; one sliced 900 bytes of source and asserted against the window, which found the wrong region and went red on correct code.
to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19. perry-goals' writer moves to a store under TASK-092, so its open findings about cell escaping and the create/amend split stop applying to OKR.md — a JSON string carries a line break without a guard. WHAT STILL APPLIES: the flag-naming in refusals, and the module-scope handler class of bug, neither of which is about markdown. Re-scope when TASK-092 lands.

title: Split perry-task by subcommand group
from: NOW BLOCKED ON TASK-038 AS WELL AS TASK-065, and the reason is not the line count. MEASURED at 34bd472: class Board is 446 lines of perry-task's 3,291 (13.6 percent); the write side TASK-038 deletes — ensure_columns, ensure_section, ensure_section_columns, append_row, append_section_row, replace_row, remove_row, last_row — is 152 lines, 4.6 percent. The read side, 273 lines, STAYS, because KR-O2.2 requires a hand edit to raise a reconcile prompt rather than be overwritten, and detecting a hand edit means reading the board. So the audit's 'the write-side half of 531 plus 437 lines' overstates it: 152 lines alone would NOT justify blocking this row. THE REAL OVERLAP IS STRUCTURAL. This row's own gate says the three-way atomic write (board row + journal line + event) and the single project lock must stay single, and that a split giving two files their own commit path is worse than the file being long. After TASK-038 there IS no three-way write — one append, one render. Splitting 22 subcommands around an invariant that is about to be replaced means the split's one hard decision gets made twice. That is this row's own argument about TASK-065, one level up, applied to itself.
to: RECONSIDER UNDER ADR-007 2026-08-19. Splitting perry-task by subcommand group was sized against a tool that parses and writes markdown. Under ADR-007 that tool loses its board reader, its row renderer and its cell escaping — TASK-090, 094 and 095 between them. The split may be unnecessary at the smaller size, or may want different seams. Do not start this before TASK-095; sizing a refactor against code that is about to be deleted is how a refactor becomes wasted.

title: perry-task: Top risks becomes a table with id / opened / cleared
from: RE-REVIEWED 2026-08-18, and the root cause was WORSE than reported: FOUR implementations of 'where is this section', not three, giving three different answers in one call. On a board whose heading reads ## **Top risks** — a human bolding a heading, which no rule forbids — parse_board saw no section (0 risks), ensure_section saw none either so risk-add APPENDED A SECOND ## Top risks at exit 0, and the id minter read the rows by a third rule and numbered from them. Every risk already recorded became invisible to every tool and perry-lint said nothing. FIXED: one predicate, viewer/parsers.py heading_is, decoration-tolerant via the same squash the header cells use; bin/perry-task gains heading_matches sharing it; ensure_section and named_section and has_section route through it. THE FOURTH was found by fixing the other three and re-running — top_risks_section had a regex of its own, so the reader still reported zero after the writer was fixed. Verified end to end on the bolded shape: 0 to 2 risks seen before the write, one section after it, 3 risks after, and risk-clear can address the earlier ids again. tests/test_one_heading_predicate.py asserts all four agree across 7 decorated spellings including Chinese, and keeps the boundary the old regex protected (## P2 must not match ## P20). 4 mutations red; a fifth came back green because it undid only one of the two places the fix touched, and was redone against the predicate itself. AWAITING a fresh V4.

from: FOUND 2026-08-18 while fixing TASK-044's planning crash, by asserting what I ASSUMED rather than what happens — the test failed and the code was right. write_atomic writes a .tmp and calls Path.replace, and A RENAME NEEDS WRITE PERMISSION ON THE DIRECTORY, NOT ON THE TARGET. So a file the user has chmod-ed read-only is migrated like any other, and nothing in the plan says the bit was there. THE QUESTION IS A POLICY ONE ABOUT SOMEBODY ELSE'S FILES and I deliberately did not decide it mid-fix: (a) the bit is an explicit user signal and ADR-004's whole posture is 'the user declares', so migration should refuse or at least name it; (b) it may be incidental — copied off a read-only medium, or a stale mode from an archive — and refusing would block a migration for a reason unrelated to shape. PINNED BY A TEST TODAY: the file IS migrated, and the restore point carries its original bytes, so the recovery path covers it — which is what makes the current behaviour survivable rather than merely undetected. NOT TRUE TODAY: that the plan mentions the mode at all. Whichever way this is decided, TASK-044-spec says migration is 'not silent — every file it touched, listed, with what changed in each', and a permission it overrode belongs in that list.

reason: The measurement this row asked for was made (TASK-110) and it argues against the row. The whole proposal recovers 560,089 bytes — 1.4 days of growth at the measured 405,349 bytes/day — once, and nothing in it keeps pace. The cost is also not paid where the bytes are: perry-lint reads all 135 evidence files in 8ms and no agent loads evidence/ per turn. Rule B's selector decays; rule A deletes the argument history a project that reviews this hard depends on. The lever the measurement does point at is how much prose a V4 round emits, which is a product decision, not this row. Dropped on the evidence, not for lack of interest.

title: When migration encounters a file the user has chmod-ed read-only, should it refuse to touch that file, or migrate it and name the overridden permission in the plan? Today it migrates silently: write_atomic renames over the target, and a rename needs write permission on the directory, not on the file.
answer: Migrate and name the override; do not refuse. Reasoning recorded because the row was minted for it: refusing would block a whole migration for a reason unrelated to shape, and migration is the one road ADR-004 gives an undeclared project — a refusal there is the wall with no door that this project rejects everywhere else. The override is also reversible: the restore point carries the file's original bytes, verified under TASK-079. The 'at least name it' half of the ADR-004 posture is already satisfied by what shipped in PR #6, and TASK-115 added the guard that keeps that wording an observation rather than advice. The read-only bit stays a signal Perry reports and does not act on.

TASK-203 has now failed THREE V4 rounds, all three mine, and every one has ended with the same defect: an ordinary command silently truncates a canonical register store. I said I would escalate rather than attempt a fourth, so here it is. ROUND 3's FAIL: the gate is read at a moment the command controls. cmd_add's queue-mode branch calls ensure_section('Intake') BEFORE commit() asks the gate, so the gate sees a freshly created, readable, EMPTY table, answers yes, derives [] and writes zero bytes. Measured: a 291-byte 3-record intake.jsonl goes to 0 on 'perry-task add --track ops' with rc 0, byte-identical on 45a355d, and perry-lint reports '0 row(s) drifted'. It is round 1's blocking finding word for word — round 2 closed it for the project-mode track and never asked the queue-mode track, which is the mode ## Intake exists for. Three more doors of the same shape: intake 3->1, ask 3->1, risk-add 3->1, all rc 0, all preserved on base. THE DECISION. (A) Evaluate the gate against the board AS IT WAS AT COMMAND ENTRY, not after the command mutated it — snapshot the shape before any board write. Principled and small, but it is the fourth 'move the question' fix on this row and the first three all looked principled too. (B) RECOMMENDED — make it structurally impossible: an ordinary write may never SHRINK a canonical store. Only an explicit removal command (purge, resolve-intake, intake-sweep) may reduce the record count, and any derivation that would produce fewer records than the store holds is a refusal, not a write. That is one invariant covering every door found in three rounds — the command name, the non-unique tuple, the four section shapes, and the ensure_section ordering — instead of a fourth predicate. (C) Revert TASK-203 entirely and reconsider the row. It has introduced a store-truncation regression in all three rounds; before it, intake.jsonl did not exist and could not be wrong. That is a real 'should we do this at all' question and it deserves an answer, not an assumption. (D) Narrow the scope to the risks register only, which is the one that already existed, and defer intake/asks. NOTE THIS AFFECTS THE PHASE: TASK-203 is the ONLY row under P003-O1-KR1, and DoD Must-Have 2 names intake.jsonl and asks.jsonl explicitly, so (C) or (D) means the phase misses that Must-Have deliberately rather than by accident. title: perry-decide REISSUES a retired ADR id, and perry-task does not — two tools, one contract, opposite answers. Measured by the TASK-235 agent 2026-08-29: delete ADR-011's file and the next mint hands out 011 again. perry-task purge retires an id through the append-only event log so it is never reissued; perry-decide writes NO events at all, so it has nothing to retire an id with. Worse, before TASK-235 the behaviour was NON-DETERMINISTIC: on main an unrelated write re-rendered the index and the next mint reissued anyway. THE STAKE: an ADR id is an address. ADR-007 is cited by name in ADR-010, in DESIGN-013, in three task rows and in this project's own commit messages. If 011 can name two different decisions, every one of those citations becomes ambiguous the moment an ADR is deleted and a new one minted. This did not matter while nobody deleted ADRs; TASK-235 is the row that made deletion ordinary. THE OPTIONS. (a) RECOMMENDED — perry-decide writes events like every other writer, and an id is retired the way perry-task retires one. This is the answer that makes the two tools agree rather than documenting why they differ, and DESIGN-004's whole posture is that every write goes through a tool and leaves a trace. Cost: perry-decide gains an event surface it does not have today. (b) Refuse the delete instead: an ADR file may not be removed, only superseded — which is arguably what a decision record SHOULD mean, since ADR-005 and ADR-007 are cited as history and history is not deleted. Cheaper, and it may be more correct in principle. (c) Accept reissue, and document that an ADR id is a slot rather than an address. Honest but it silently breaks every existing citation. (d) Leave it declared as it is now — the TASK-235 agent pinned the disagreement with a named test rather than resolving it silently, so nothing is hidden and the row can close. My recommendation is (b) THEN (a): stop the deletion that creates the problem, then give perry-decide the event surface so the two tools stop disagreeing on principle rather than by accident. But (b) changes what a decision record IS, which is yours and not mine.
